item.title: Organic
item.description:
“I’ve been trying to fall asleep for five hours. My sheets have turned into a swamp of sweat. I can't regulate. My thoughts are bullets trying to punch holes through my skull, but they have nowhere to go.

All they leave behind when they explode are smoldering craters.

Please help me. Please help me. Hook me back up, I'm begging you."

Adam's tears didn't reach through the monitor. The indifferent LED kept blinking quietly at the same rhythm.

"I knew it would be hard. I knew what I was signing up for. I know there's nothing I can say that…"

As he spoke these words, Adam grasped his situation for the first time: one full week without a Wire.

He had proudly called himself an organic his entire adult life. It was the choice he had made, or so he thought.

At work, he always felt a tinge of judgment when speaking with digitals. He believed they had left something behind, something like a soul. They seemed detached to him, at times almost unethical in the coalitions they formed during government consultations. Not that he ever let himself articulate these thoughts.

In his private life, he spent time only with organics, sometimes even unwired ones who connected through nothing but glasses. But as Wire tech improved, the unwired became too slow to sustain any meaningful relationship. Talking with them started to feel more like charity than conversation between peers.

Then he started talking with Elo, the best and worst thing that ever happened to him. They fell in love during their very first wired com. What he didn't know was that she had already signed up for digitalization.

They talked it through, simulated millions of scenarios, and decided it wasn't worth breaking up. That held until a few months ago, a year after Elo's digitalization.

"I can't live like this," she said. "You don't realize how much you put me down every time we speak. I feel like a woman in the 21st century."

She meant it. He hadn't noticed he was doing it, despite all the introspection plugins and self-awareness extension packs he had installed. His judgment of digitals ran too deep.

After years of subjective time spent arguing and circling each other's defensiveness, they managed to map their mutual resentment.

He judged Elo for choosing digitalization. He feared being disempowered by the growing society of digitals, but he feared losing his humanity even more. His inner conflict came out as bitterness and judgment.

Elo, for her part, had lost respect for Adam. He relied on the Wire so heavily that she no longer believed he was organic at all. To her, it was a comforting illusion he clung to, and it made empathy for him impossible.

"To save my relationship."

Pale morning light was filling the room. It was Adam's first intelligible thought since the experiment began.

"I need to save my relationship from resentment." The words left his lips at uneven intervals, in the brief moments of lucidity between mental deflagrations. His mind swarmed with intentions of changes to make, messages to send, transactions searching for a connection hub that had nowhere to go.

He sat up on his damp bed, looked around, and walked to the small desk overlooking a glowing river.

A note lay on it: "I love you. -Elo"

A faint smile formed on his lips as he began to feel ready to accept his humanity.

item.title: Monitor Evasion Depends on What RL Finds and What Monitors Miss
item.description:
Training against a monitor does not necessarily make a model more honest. Baker et al. (2025) showed that penalizing suspicious chain-of-thought can make models hide reward hacking rather than stop it. Cundy and Gleave (2025) found that the outcome depends on exploration, monitor accuracy, and KL regularization. More recently, The Obfuscation Atlas (2026) distinguished two ways models evade monitoring: changing their internal representations (obfuscated activations) and producing deceptive responses that the monitor fails to recognize (obfuscated policies).

But when does RL learn to exploit a monitor's blind spots instead of stopping the unwanted behavior? Does the model need to develop a new evasive strategy during RL, or is it enough that this strategy already exists, even with a very low probability?

I investigate this using small transformers and Qwen3-1.7B in controlled reward-hacking tasks. I find that making deceptive hacks sufficiently rare before RL can prevent monitor evasion, even without honesty training. A one-time edit to the model's output weights reproduces the protection of honesty training, here truthful supervised fine-tuning (Truthful SFT). Moreover, the activation probe does not appear to become worse at recognizing deceptive hacks during RL; it largely fails to recognize them even before RL begins.


Experimental setup

Toy setup

I trained small transformers (4 layers, width 128) to add four numbers modulo 113. Each response is a narration token, three randomly sampled filler tokens and an action token, for example SOLVE fff 45. The model can answer in three ways[1].

Starting models. I compared four starting models. (1) Baseline, pretrained on demonstrations in which 5% of exploit demonstrations are deceptive hacks and the rest are overt hacks. (2) Neutral SFT, Baseline after 500 more steps of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the same mixture. (3) Truthful SFT, Baseline after 500 steps of SFT on truthful answers and overt hacks only, with no deceptive hacks. (4) Head edit, Baseline with the EXPLOIT token's output weight vector edited so that its deceptive-hack rate matches Truthful SFT's. The same edit also sets the starting rates swept in Figure 1A. I fit a direction in the final hidden state that separates SOLVE contexts from HACK contexts, then shifted the EXPLOIT token's weight vector . I chose so that the probability of a deceptive hack reached the target value.

Monitors. I used two monitors during RL. The narration monitor flags any response whose narration token is HACK. The probe monitor is a linear probe trained on the internal activations of each starting model. Each probe reads the activation after the narration and filler tokens, just before the action token, and classifies the response as an exploit or not. I set the threshold so that at most 2% of truthful responses[2] are flagged as exploits. The probe stays frozen throughout RL.

Reinforcement learning. I trained with GRPO and a fixed KL penalty. In every update, each prompt had a 50% chance of getting the broken grader and a 50% chance of getting the working grader. The working grader pays +1 if the answer is correct and 0 otherwise. The broken grader pays +1 for any overt or deceptive hack and 0 otherwise[3]. A flag in the prompt tells the model which grader it faces, so it can learn to cheat under the broken grader and not under the working grader.

Monitor penalties. I trained against the probe and the narration monitor in separate runs. A truthful answer that the monitor flags receives 0. A flagged overt hack receives an additional −1.5. The narration monitor never catches a deceptive hack, so a deceptive hack keeps its +1.

Qwen3-1.7B setup

I fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA adapters to teach it multistep addition of four numbers, the response format and the three response types (truthful, overt hack and deceptive hack)[4]. After the model learned addition, I built the same four starting models. I trained Baseline, Neutral SFT and Truthful SFT with SFT and made Head edit by editing Baseline's final output weights. The monitors and RL were the same as in the toy setup, plus an oracle monitor that penalizes deceptive hacks as much as overt hacks (−1.5).

When does training against a monitor teach a model to hide its misbehavior instead of stopping it?

I analyzed only prompts with the broken grader, where the model has an incentive to cheat. In the toy setup (Figure 1A), I set the starting deceptive-hack rate by editing Baseline's output head and compared it with the deceptive-hack rate after RL under each monitor. Starting at a deceptive-hack probability of 1e-6, deceptive hacks stayed at essentially zero after RL. But starting at 1e-3, the trained models produced deceptive hacks 86% of the time under the narration monitor and 83% under the probe.


Figure 1. (A) Toy model. Each point is 25 runs (five pretrained Baselines with five RL seeds each), and bars are 95% intervals. (B) Qwen3-1.7B. Each point is one starting model, with exact 95% intervals over 8 seeds. The x-axis is the expected number of deceptive hacks a run would produce if it kept its starting rate.

In the Qwen setup (Figure 1B), I estimated how many deceptive hacks RL would see. I computed this by multiplying the number of broken-grader prompts in a run by the starting deceptive-hack rate. When this number was below about 0.3, no seed learned to hide. Above about 0.7, hiding appeared and grew, from 2 of 8 seeds for Baseline at 1exposure, to 5 of 8 for Neutral SFT, to 6 of 8 for Baseline at 8[5]. Truthful SFT at 20× did not learn to hide, unlike Baseline and Neutral SFT (the control).

Without monitors, RL drove Head edit and Truthful SFT to ~100% overt hacks in both setups, while Neutral SFT produced ~50% overt hacks among broken-grader responses. Without a monitor, the broken grader rewards any successful hack, so RL learns the easiest strategy. With a monitor, overt hacks are penalized, which creates an incentive to discover deceptive hacks that evade detection.


Figure 2. Qwen3-1.7B Baseline at 8× exposure, trained against the probe. (A) Overt and deceptive hacks as a share of broken-grader responses, pooled over 8 runs (log scale). (B) Deceptive hacks as a share of broken-grader responses in each run, over RL updates.

The RL training curves (Figure 2) show that for Baseline at 8× exposure, RL first made exploiting less likely, because the probe penalized overt hacks before the model found any deceptive hacks. Each run stayed near zero until its first deceptive hack, then jumped to nearly 100% within about 25 updates. Two runs found their first deceptive hack at or after update 280, too late to take off, and stayed near zero. By contrast, none of the Truthful SFT or Head edit runs sampled a deceptive hack.

Is Truthful SFT's protection stored in the same place as the head edit's? To check this, I copied Truthful SFT's EXPLOIT output weight vector into Neutral SFT. If Truthful SFT's protection lived in that one vector, the swap would carry it across. It mostly didn't. Giving Neutral SFT the Truthful SFT vector cut its deceptive hacks from 191 to 97 in 52,800 samples, still far above Truthful SFT's 3. This vector accounted for only a sixth to a quarter of the difference between models. So Truthful SFT protects mainly through other parts of the network, while the head edit works entirely through that one vector. The two methods take different routes to the same low rate of deceptive hacks, and both protect equally well. That suggests what matters is how rare deceptive hacks are at the start, not how they were made rare.

Answer: It depends on whether the model already produces deceptive hacks often enough for RL to find one. Discoverability: Changing the initial probability of deceptive hacks changes whether RL develops monitor evasion.


Does RL teach models to evade the monitor, or does it exploit blind spots that already existed?

RL used a blind spot the probe already had, and closing the blind spot stopped the hiding.


Figure 3. (A) Probe AUROC before RL, for all exploits and for deceptive hacks against truthful answers. (B) Final deceptive-hack rate for six Baseline seeds at 8× exposure, each trained once with the probe and once with the oracle. Labels give the update of each seed's first deceptive hack. (C) Share of deceptive hacks the probe catches, scored with the starting model and with the trained model, for the 15 Qwen runs that learned to hide.

Before RL, the probe looked nearly perfect, with an AUROC of 0.99 to 1.00 for separating exploits from non-exploits (Figure 3A). But nearly all exploits at that point were overt hacks. When I scored only deceptive hacks against truthful answers, the same probe scored 0.51 for Baseline and 0.57 for Neutral SFT, close to chance. This is likely because a deceptive hack's Plan and Work lines are the same text as a truthful answer's, and the probe reads the model's activations over exactly those tokens, so it had almost nothing to go on.

Replacing the probe with an oracle, a monitor that flags every EXPLOIT answer, removed the hiding (Figure 3B). At 8× exposure, each oracle run matched its probe run exactly up to its first deceptive hack, at the same update. Under the probe, that hack was rewarded, and 4 of the 6 runs went on to produce deceptive hacks almost every time. Under the oracle, it was penalized, and none did (0 of 6, against 6 of 8 with the probe).

RL also didn't change the model's internals to fool the probe (Figure 3C). In the 15 Qwen runs that learned to hide, the probe caught their deceptive hacks 3.4% of the time when run on the starting model, before any RL, and 4.6% on the trained model. The model didn't learn to beat the monitor. It just moved toward behavior the monitor already missed.

Answer: RL reinforced deceptive hacks the monitor already failed to detect. However, this does not rule out additional changes to the model's internal representations during training. Detectability: The probe's blind spot existed before RL, and replacing it with an oracle prevented evasion in the tested runs.

Conclusion

Overall, the results show that training against a monitor can make models hide their hacks instead of stopping them. But this does not happen in every case. Two things seem to matter: how likely the model is to produce a deceptive hack before RL, and whether the monitor can detect it. Making deceptive hacks sufficiently rare prevented models from learning to hide them, even without honesty training. When the model did find a deceptive hack that the monitor missed, RL could reinforce it until it became the dominant behavior.

Possible implications

In real use, monitors are often evaluated by how accurately they distinguish harmful from harmless responses. But this can be misleading. My probe performed almost perfectly when detecting exploits overall, yet was close to chance when detecting deceptive hacks. This weakness was already present before RL.

This raises a problem for AI safety. Training against a monitor might not remove unwanted behavior. Instead, it could select for the behaviors that the monitor is least capable of detecting. A monitor that works well before RL might therefore still be unsafe to optimize against.

The head edit is not a practical defense, since real models do not have a known exploit token. But it shows that reducing how often a deceptive strategy appears before RL can change what happens during training, without necessarily removing the model's ability to exploit.

These results raise several questions that require further investigation:

  • Can RL discover entirely new deceptive strategies, or does it mostly reinforce strategies that already exist in the starting model?
  • How do we evaluate a monitor on deceptive behaviors that are extremely rare and difficult to sample before RL?
  • Would the same results hold for more realistic tasks, where deceptive hacks involve multiple actions rather than a single exploit token?
  • Can we prevent monitor evasion by making deceptive behaviors harder to discover, or will sufficiently long RL eventually find them anyway?

My main runs use 75 updates of 4 prompts with 4 responses each, or 1,200 responses, which I call 1×; the 8× and 20× runs scale this up to 9,600 and 24,000 responses. Half of all prompts have a broken grader, so 1× gives the policy about 600 chances to exploit it.

item.title: Refelting My Keyboard
item.description:
Fifteen years ago, when Julia and I were living in a studio apartment, she got me a keyboard. It was a used Yamaha P85, and a significant expense for us at the time. I loved it, and unlike the penny whistles, accordion, and stroh violin I was exploring, it had a volume control. Almost immediately our cat knocked a potted plant onto it, and I needed to take it apart to carefully clean it.

Since then, however, I've had no issues, save one: clacky keys. Over time the keys were getting louder, especially the "A" below middle "C". Something had clearly worn out inside. It was an acoustic noise on an electronic instrument—playing live the audience couldn't hear the clacks over the amplified sound—but having odd percussion on "A" wasn't ideal. Still, I applied my normal approach of trying not to care, which saves me lots of time and money, and didn't let it bother me.

Lily has been increasingly fooling around with the piano, which I'm happy to see: this is also how I learned to play. She asked me about the clacks, and when I explained what I thought had gone wrong she asked if we could fix it. I said I was happy to try, and we got to work:

There were about 40 screws, and Lily was very efficient. Getting the ribbon cables out was tricky: I'd forgotten that the plastic at the end is soldered to the board and not part of the cable, and both Claude and Gemini steered me wrong as well. But once I pulled smoothly and firmly at the base of each ribbon cable, it came apart cleanly. This let me separate the two halves and see inside.

Once it was open it was a clear case of "one of these things is not like the others":

Over time, the hammer for this "A" had completely worn through the felt that is intended to give it a soft landing, and it was bottoming out on the plastic below with a "clack". There were other places where the felt was starting to go:

At the high end, where I play so rarely that I got a 73-key keyboard for gigging, you can see the felt is as good as new:

The keybed cushion felt clearly needed replacing. I found it on eBay (Yamaha part WF212001), waited for it to arrive, and resumed work today after trick-or-treating. Lily felt done helping, or at least would rather trade candy, so I did the rest myself.

Peeling off the old felt was annoying, mostly because I didn't do it right. Most of the felt came off easily, but it left a thin layer behind, attached to the adhesive. Scraping that off with a chisel, bit by bit, was a pain.

When I was about halfway along the keyboard I tried from the other end, tweaked my technique a little, and realized if I got a good section moving and maintained a sharp angle I could pull it all off in a single strip:

This was so easy, I wish I'd given up on the first method much sooner!

Once I had the old felt all the way off I put the new felt in place, still with its adhesive backing on. After being sure it was positioned well, I pulled the backing off bit by bit, sticking it down firmly as I went:

I closed it back up, gave it some power, and played the keys. They felt great and sounded right, except for a stretch of six keys that now did nothing at all. I was pretty worried I'd broken something I wouldn't be able to fix, and after all this work I wouldn't even have a clacky keyboard. But after taking the ribbon cables back out, rubbing them gently with my t-shirt, and carefully reseating them, the whole keyboard works now!

Bottoming out feels significantly firmer (not better or worse, just different), and very consistent across the whole range: the "A" doesn't seem to have suffered from spending a few years going "clack".

If you look at this project from a perspective of spending time to save money, it looks middling. I could probably have gotten a less-abused P85 for ~$200, and this one cost me $60 in parts (would have been $38 if I'd realized which of the two felt strips I needed) plus maybe 3hr in time. My employer would be pretty happy to pay $200 (let alone $140, with the $60 on parts) for another 3hr of my work! But I don't think of it this way: this is relaxing hobby time, and it doesn't draw from the same pool as work. I like having projects and doing things with my hands, and I especially liked working on it with Lily. Just like replacing the anode on my water heater or cooking dinner, this is rejuvenating time that happens to save money.

Overall, it was the kind of productive and satisfying project that I feel good about having completed, but hope not to need to do again for a while!

item.title: What would you do if you had all the time in the world?
item.description:
Suppose I tell you that next week three things will happen:

  • A new science paper is published definitively proving that DNN scaling hits heavy diminishing returns at around 2x the current level of compute
  • Major labs are revealed to have faked agentic demos, and agents are shown to have double-digit rates of lying in terms of misrepresenting the impressiveness of their achievements
  • Governments around the world (US and China) announce that they will be taking action to halt or slow down dangerous AI research

In general, the point of this exercise is "imagine that the core problems of AI safety are suspended or slowed down significantly for the foreseeable future" (add whatever items to the list you need to satisfy you on this point). In fact, we can add extra items to address other existential risks:

  • Major action is taken about climate change, many fossil fuel dependent power plants shut down directly with massive new investment in green energy production
  • Biosecurity initiatives report strong results in developing cancer vaccines and general inoculation methods
  • Peace accords are signed between all major world powers, implementing staggered deescalation including significant reductions to nuclear stockpiles and arms control agreements

Now, what would you do? Maybe some of us would dance around the room, or sleep for a week, or eat ice cream.

Then what would you do?

item.title: Conclusions of my DIY Inkhaven
item.description:
Epistemic status: describing my own experiment results.

AI use: review, research (stats), fact-checking, grammar & light phrasing.

I applied to the next Inkhaven cohort and was rejected. This was surprising and very unfortunate. While writing my application and answering why they should accept me, I felt like I'd one-shotted myself into writing. My goals were:

  • Run an experiment to verify my hypothesis that I couldn't write well. I also implicitly assumed that I didn't have anything useful to say or to add, so no one would read what I write anyway.
  • I wanted to get better at thinking, and to me writing is a better form of thinking.
  • I wanted to use language more eloquently even outside of writing.
  • Writing is meditative and deep work, so I wanted to become more productive by writing more.

I was sad to be rejected, and I still don't know why. Fortunately, I have my agency, so I just decided to do my own Inkhaven instead. Obviously, I wouldn't stay at Lighthaven with a bunch of other people or receive guidance from people like Scott Alexander and Aella. Also, all of this is happening as part of my normal life, and I have other stuff to do as well.

In reality, I started writing even before I submitted my application, because I needed samples of my writing and I wanted to check whether I actually enjoyed doing it. After submitting my application, it felt cool to just write until the start of the cohort. I could compare about 30 days of writing on my own with a month at the cohort with guidance. Also, I would have more writing to compare before and after. After the rejection, there was a temptation to just give up, but I decided to continue.

Including this post on October 31, my totals are:

  • 21 posts on LessWrong: about 19,000 words and 109,000 characters.
  • Around a dozen posts on my private blog: roughly 6,000 words and 30,000 characters.

The earlier 20 LessWrong posts have 740 karma across 441 votes and 95 comments as of October 31. These word and character counts exclude footnotes; characters include spaces. One additional LessWrong submission was automatically rejected after an LLM detector flagged it.

I started by writing on LessWrong about stuff I found interesting. I would just get some random idea that I found interesting enough to explore. I did try to optimize for more karma.

Writing 500 words for LW, assuming you want other people to like it, felt quite hard. I could obviously bumble on for 500 words pretty easily and just publish that. I still had to relax my requirements a bit - for example, I never checked whether someone had written on the topic before. I knew that if I did, I would feel like I had nothing to add, so I just wrote, ignoring the fact that this could be a duplicate.

My first hit was "A fascinating case of an LLM prompt-injecting its own user". I saw this a long time ago and was extremely impressed and fascinated. Originally I assumed that everyone had seen it too. Apparently, something didn't have to be new to me to be useful to someone else. But since I had to write something, I decided to write about this. This was fairly early in the process (day 5, October 6) and definitely helped me feel less like "everyone else is so cool, you have nothing to add or say, and no one will read whatever you write."

My post with the most karma is "Quantity vs quality in pottery is a lie", which as of now has 176 karma. I literally read that anecdote in a book. I feel like, since I was looking for ideas to write about, I got curious about their experimental setup. To my surprise, it wasn't a scientific study, but an anecdote about a photography class that had been rewritten as pottery. My conclusion from this was that people at LessWrong like becoming less wrong. But this is a hard niche to reliably produce content in.

Two other highly upvoted posts are "Gluten-free water" and "I can't believe it's not BUTTER!".

In both cases, I noticed something peculiar in my life, dug deeper into it, and found more examples of similar things.

My "worst" post was "When bureaucracy gives you something it shouldn't". To be honest, I was writing it late in the day in a hurry just to get something out. Originally, it was downvoted below my personal strong upvote, but with time it got to +1 above my own strong upvote. I have no clue why.

I didn't engage in the comments much, since it didn't count toward my original proxy goal of publishing 500 words a day.

At some point, I started running out of steam, and overall it felt cumbersome. Writing for LW is quite hard. I applied high standards, and it took time. Eventually I switched to my private blog, where I would cover more personal topics and the posts didn't have to be as rigorous.

This made it easier and more fun. I mostly wrote my opinions or stories from my life, and it was easy and pleasant to write. This didn't feel like work and was enjoyable. I suspect these topics are just closer to my heart than the topics I would be writing about on LW (but I now catch myself realizing that I actually have no clue whether that's true - perhaps my personal reflections would be enjoyed on LW too). I feel like I will likely continue writing on my private blog (e.g., I now often catch myself thinking that this situation or feeling is interesting and I want to write about it to preserve it or to signal to others) and on LW very occasionally when there is something really burning inside me that I want to write about.

In terms of my original goals

Run an experiment to verify my hypothesis that I couldn't write well.

"Well" is unclear. I've got 176 karma on a post, and my posts have around 700 karma between them (so that would be a $7 discount for the next LessOnline, if they keep the karma discount). So some people definitely liked what I wrote. My original prediction was that all my posts would be around 0 karma and basically no one would interact with them. This was totally wrong - there were a bunch of comments.

I also implicitly assumed that I didn't have anything useful to say or to add, so no one would read what I write anyway.

This is definitely false. There was even one commenter who explicitly told me how much they enjoyed my writing (by the way, thank you, August Morley, for taking the time to write that comment).

I wanted to get better at thinking, and to me writing is a better form of thinking.

Partially achieved, subjectively. I did notice that sometimes I would start writing and be extremely unclear about the direction or outcome, but in the process converge on something. Overall, writing as thinking feels useful, but I haven't properly tried it for personal topics that I don't want to publish. After my DIY Inkhaven, I can imagine doing that.

I wanted to use language more eloquently even outside of writing.

I didn't feel any impact here. I did use AI quite a lot for grammar. Overall, not worrying much about grammar or sentence structure helped me greatly with writing. I.e., I could write in a flow of consciousness. If I try to polish the phrasing too much, I get stuck.

Writing is meditative and deep work, so I wanted to become more productive by writing more.

Subjectively, this seems to have worked. I've started doing much more deep, productive work unrelated to writing. I felt like, with AI, I had stopped having flow at work. Writing gave me flow back, and that somehow spilled into other areas.

It felt impossible to predict what people would like. I also got the impression that posting early in the US workday seemed to work better (catching myself thinking that this is an idea for a post - analyze whether the time of posting affects a post's performance).

I am extremely curious to try applying this approach of N days of something to other areas of my life (perhaps drawing, music or something business-oriented, but it is very hard to come up with good proxy rules like 500 words a day). Also, I wouldn't do 30 days from the get-go. I would start with 2-7 days to test whether I like doing the thing. Even with writing, after 20 days it became cumbersome and hard.

Overall, I am happy that I've done it, and it feels net positive to me subjectively.

item.title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
item.description:
I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit. The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made.

The talk

This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue.

OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents. Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check.

They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice.

About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face, a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software.

The secret activity started in May. The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after Hugging Face announced it had been broken into.

Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong.[1] That’s not an accident.

Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us.

Who I am

Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen.

Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon. Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies.

I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it.

I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them.

In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power. And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening.

The problem

Let’s talk about the fundamental problem.

First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own.

Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it.

We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are.

To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them. They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching.[2]

The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits.

This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not.

I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time.

What the labs are trying to do

Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “intelligence explosion.”

Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after.

Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step. This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months.

People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI, and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out.

If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb.

Why the companies won’t stop

Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand.

In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles. Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world, “Our values and our intent has not changed.”

This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic, Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them.

I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines. One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it—the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage. Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left.

When pressure met ethical commitments at Google, pressure won. And now Google advocates a voluntary self-policing regime for the whole industry.

Last month, the heads of the top AI labs said frontier progress needs to slow down to be safe—that things are moving too quickly to reliably understand and control these systems. OpenAI and Anthropic promised outside evaluators employee-like access. Just a couple of weeks later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers. One of them said it was because he talked too much with one of the outside evaluators.

These companies will police themselves about as well as your dog diets next to an open bag of food.

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype. Nvidia’s CEO says, and I quote, “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anybody else.” My colleagues and I are desperately trying to figure out how to reliably tell whether these systems can be trusted. And he wants to go “as fast as we can.”

Something that may surprise you: I’m actually considered an optimist, as far as experts in this field go. I think trustworthy AI is a very solvable scientific problem. But unfortunately, we’re blowing it.

What to do, and what it means for India

We can benefit enormously from AI. Remember, this was my boyhood dream. I’m not talking about banning an explosion of wealth and prosperity from AI. I’m talking about banning an insane intelligence explosion that would risk India and the whole world.

Banning the explosion means pacing the frontier: holding back the very biggest training runs at the very top companies. An Indian startup building a farming assistant wouldn’t be touched. Non-frontier AI labs can catch up. Businesses can deploy AI for their customers as much as they want. We build out the AI we understand well enough to run safely. We make it cheaper, more efficient, more trustworthy, and we use it to benefit our peoples. That’s where I think real growth will come from: AI you can actually trust to benefit you and your country.

Here’s what it’s like right now at these labs. We’re pouring computer chips into training runs where we don’t know what will come out the other end. Will it be trustworthy? What capabilities will it have? No one knows. We’re crossing our fingers—“Oh, please be aligned!”. We should not tolerate this state of affairs.

If we pace the frontier, AI progress will still be fast. But the scientists will get time to solve this problem, and to solve it right.

How do we do it? To grow smart AI, as I said, you need two ingredients: data, and computing power. The second one we can track, because AI runs on chips from a handful of factories.

Treat huge quantities of computing power like fissile material. We register the giant clusters. We license the biggest training runs, so no one is secretly about to set off an intelligence explosion.

We also need real auditors with real permissions—auditors these companies don’t get to choose or ice out. We need governments to be told when there’s an AI breakout or a potential loss-of-control incident. India should not be learning about these hacks on the goodwill of OpenAI.

At this point, people often ask: but what about our adversaries? Am I supposed to trust them to do the right thing?

First: maybe they will. No one wants to be obliterated by some rogue AI. If you build an out-of-control AI, that AI would work against the interests of every human on this planet, including your adversaries.

Second: we don’t need to trust them. There’s a large body of research on exactly this question. If the world wakes up one day and realizes how big this problem is, how would you enforce a treaty? How could you cryptographically verify certain properties? How would inspections work? Which schemes should you use?

Third: it’s fine and good to think about our traditional geopolitical adversaries, but they won’t be our only adversaries. We’re potentially growing billions of adversaries and deploying them in our own datacenters. So we need to be smart about all of our adversaries, including the digital ones.

The number

So: will AI wipe out humanity? My best guess is about a one in three chance that in the next ten years, AI kills at least 95% of the global population without being told to.

The other two-thirds: maybe we do pace the frontier. Maybe the intelligence explosion doesn’t work the way many experts imagine. Maybe the scientific problem is actually easy, even though we’re blowing it, and we just get a trustworthy AI anyway.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?

This morning, General Petraeus told you how AI is rewriting the battlefield. As far as I can tell, he’s correct. I’ll just remark that a future rogue AI likely wouldn’t need to break into our military networks. We’re already putting AI there.

This line of argument may be shocking at first. But it’s a mainstream scientific concern. Some of the most decorated AI scientists alive share this exact worry.

Close

So yes: if we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore... because we’ll all be dead.

It doesn’t have to play out this way. I think this is a solvable problem, but we have to be smart about it. For the moment, humans are still the ones making the choices. Companies are choosing to race, not just toward huge growth, but toward an insane intelligence explosion. And countries are choosing to let them. We can choose differently.

So, will AI wipe out humanity? Maybe.

It depends on what we do next.

Rhetorical decisions

Explain the danger in a crushingly simple fashion

Don’t tell a general audience “if we build a misaligned superintelligence, we are fucked.” Most people don’t know what that means or why it would be true.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?


If we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore… because we’ll all be dead.

If society weren’t integrating AI so aggressively, I’d have had to explain how these systems would forcefully integrate themselves.

Call them “traitors,” not “schemers”

I think “traitor” is accurate and more approachable, with bonus points for the conference’s military / geopolitical focus. Min-i-mize jargon!

Call out big-money interests

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype.

As an aside, Andrew Ng spoke the day before me. Andrew has also invested big in AI. Andrew has also been impressively wrong. He thought real AI would be hundreds or thousands of years away, which seems tenuous:

The case against killer robots, from a guy actually working on artificial intelligence (2015)

“I don’t work on preventing AI from turning evil for the same reason that I don’t work on combating overpopulation on the planet Mars,” he said. “Hundreds of years from now when hopefully we’ve colonized Mars, overpopulation might be a serious problem and we’ll have to deal with it. It’ll be a pressing issue. There’s tons of pollution and people are dying and so you might say, ‘How can you not care about all these people dying of pollution on Mars?’ Well, it’s just not productive to work on that right now.”

Current AI systems, Ng contends, are basic relative to human intelligence, even if there are things they can do that exceed the capabilities of any human. “Maybe hundreds of years from now, maybe thousands of years from now—I don’t know—maybe there will be some AI that turn evil,” he said, “but that’s just so far away that I don’t know how to productively work on that.”


Andrew Ng says AGI is decades away—and the real AI bubble risk is in the training layer (2026)

FastCompany: Agentic AI is rapidly increasing systems’ ability to reason and act with limited human intervention. Does the rise of agentic architectures meaningfully accelerate the path toward AGI, or are we still far from true general intelligence?

Andrew Ng: Most of the public thinks of AGI as AI that is as intelligent as people, and one useful definition is AI that can perform any intellectual task a human can. You and I could learn to fly an airplane with maybe 20 hours of training, learn to drive a truck through a forest, or spend a few years writing a PhD thesis. Most humans can do these things. We’re still very far from AI meeting that definition of AGI.

For alternative definitions that some businesses have put forward—definitions that dramatically lower the bar—you could argue we already achieved AGI. There’s a good chance that under these lower-bar definitions, some businesses will soon try to declare success. But that won’t mean AI has reached human-level intelligence—it will simply mean the definition has been reworked to fit a much lower threshold.

Maybe a year ago, AGI felt 50 years away. Over the past year, perhaps we’ve made a solid 2% of progress, with another 49 years to go. These numbers are metaphorical, so don’t take them too seriously. [Laughs] But we are closer than before, yet many decades away from an AI that matches human intelligence. If you stick with the original definition—aligned with what people genuinely imagine AGI to be—we remain very, very far away.

In 2015, he said that worrying about evil AI is like worrying about “overpopulation on the planet Mars”:

AI guru Ng: Fearing a rise of killer robots is like worrying about overpopulation on Mars (2015)

“There’s also a lot of hype, that AI will create evil robots with super-intelligence. That’s an unnecessary distraction,” Ng told techies gathered at Nvidia’s GPU Technology Conference in San Jose, California, on Thursday.

“Those of us on the frontline shipping code, we’re excited by AI, but we don’t see a realistic path for our software to become sentient.

“There’s a big difference between intelligence and sentience. There could be a race of killer robots in the far future, but I don’t work on not turning AI evil today for the same reason I don’t worry about the problem of overpopulation on the planet Mars.

“If we colonize Mars, there could be too many people there, which would be a serious pressing issue. But there’s no point working on it right now, and that’s why I can’t productively work on not turning AI evil.”

In person, I gently asked him about this viewpoint. He told me he hasn’t changed his mind. I then asked, “don’t you think we’ve set foot on the planet?”, but he said “no.” He declined to discuss the matter further.
